extracted.intended_audience: readers and critics of travel/colonial writing; educated West Indian and British public
extracted.subtask_description: A late-19th-century polemical essay rebutting a travelogue's claims about West Indian societies; combines historical argument, factual correction, and literary criticism. The rubric pertains to standards for accurate, fair, and effective critical writing about colonial subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: True ease in writing comes from Art, not Chance
rubrics_metrics.description: "True ease in writing comes from Art, not Chance," (quoting Alexander Pope) — writing skill is the product of craft and practice, not luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop regular practice in composition to achieve 'true ease'; do not rely on occasional inspiration. Thomas cites his own prolonged illness as a mitigating factor for stylistic defects but upholds the principle that craft produces reliable style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize verity over verbal attractiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not sacrifice truth for stylistic or verbal attractiveness; artistic perfection of style must not override veracity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing travel/critical writing, check that rhetorical flourish does not distort facts. Thomas accuses Froude of being 'the bond-slave of his own phrases' and of 'disregard[ing] ... the requirements of verity' to secure artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting prejudice shape observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic or traveller must not be 'unhampered by prejudices' that lead to biased descriptions and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of generalisations or negative characterizations that stem from preconception rather than evidence. Thomas points to Froude's racial prejudice as skewing his perceptions and reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain proportion and avoid exaggerated superlatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from disproportionate language and constant use of superlatives which distort representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer measured descriptions; excessive enthusiasm or hostility ('his enthusiasm for or against admits no degree ... the superlative') reduces reliability. Evaluate whether claims are presented with appropriate restraint and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims with impartial history and common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to impartial historical evidence and common-sense reasoning when making or rebutting broad claims about peoples or political consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas argues that the best refutation of Froude's 'negrophobic' project is to rely on impartial history, documents, oral tradition, and common-sense application to facts of West Indian life. Use multiple lines of corroboration rather than rhetoric alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reliable, local, and documentary evidence to verify factual assertions
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify factual claims (geography, demography, customs, speech, etc.) against local knowledge, documents, and authoritative testimonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas supplies concrete counter-evidence to Froude (e.g., no forest trees near the Grenada Carenage; dialect/accent claims contradicted by other eyewitness writers). Cross-check traveller claims with local witnesses, contemporary accounts (Chester, Trollope), and records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate analogies and comparators
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not manufacture or misuse analogies (e.g., treating Haiti as a standard for all Black societies) — analogies must be relevant and based on comparable circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas criticises Froude's reliance on Haiti as an analogy and suggests Liberia would be a more apt comparator in some respects. Evaluate whether the comparator shares the salient historical, social, and institutional features before generalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address specific passages precisely and in context
rubrics_metrics.description: When rebutting a text, take up the points 'exactly how, when, and where' they occur rather than vague generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote passages and respond to their precise claims and context. Thomas explicitly states he will take up Froude 'on the points whereto I demurred, exactly how, when, and where I found them.' This increases accountability and clarity in criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous sneers and ad hominem attacks
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from tack-on sneers or personal derision that do not bear on the substantive issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas faults Froude for appending a 'gratuitous and pointless sneer' to otherwise unrelated praise. Effective criticism concentrates on argument and evidence rather than gratuitous insults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use independent authoritative corroboration to strengthen credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent corroboration, especially from respected or external authorities, enhances the persuasive power of a rebuttal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas praises C. Salmon's vindication as valuable because it is the work of a European of high position not of the subject race; such independent testimonies can make refutation more persuasive to skeptical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of public responsibility when reproaching officials
rubrics_metrics.description: When reproducing criticism of public employes, accept that such publication may carry special responsibility and potential consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas notes he is aware that reproducing criticisms of colonial officials could attach special responsibility and accepts any consequence. Writers should verify allegations and be prepared to justify them publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer permanent, documented rejoinders over ephemeral press pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: Ephemeral newspaper responses are useful but may not be accessible for future reference; a permanent, documented rejoinder preserves the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas explains that though West Indian papers published refutations, collecting a permanent rebuttal (book form) makes the arguments available for later citation. For durable influence, aim for documented, citable rebuttals with sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sweeping social generalizations without demographic and temporal reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not extrapolate present-day danger or social vengeance from past slavery without taking into account demographics, mortality, generational change, and the existence (or nonexistence) of factors needed to carry out alleged consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thomas dismantles Froude's 'Danger-to-the-Whites' claim by pointing out demographic realities (age of ex-slaves, lack of surviving influential former-slaves) and logical inconsistencies. Evaluate claims about collective future behaviour with demographic and causal reasoning.
